notes.matooke: Ebitookye are cooked bananas; ekitooke is the banana plant or a bunch.
notes.amata: Amate, the pride of Ankole: fresh, soured (amacunda) or with tea.
notes.enva: The sauce eaten with the staple. Plural agreement: enva nizinuura.
notes.kiwooma: Agrees with the food: ebyokurya nibinuura, enva nizinuura.
notes.nnina: Nyine enjara, I’m hungry: you “have” hunger.
notes.amenvu: Eminekye are ripe sweet bananas, eaten raw.

guidebook.intro: Food in Ankole means bananas, millet, beans and, above all, milk. You’ll say you’re hungry, name the staples and buy and sell at the market.

tips.title: Nyine: “I have” for hunger
body: Runyankore says you **have** hunger and thirst: **Nyine enjara** (I’m hungry), **Nyine enyoota** (I’m thirsty).
**-ine** means have: **nyine** (I have), **oine** (you have), **aine** (he or she has). Add **ti-** for “not”: **Tinyine munyaanyazi** (I don’t have a sister).

tips.title: Ningura, ningurisa
body: **-gura** is to buy, and **-gurisa** is to sell: literally “make buy”. **Ningura ebitookye** (I’m buying matooke), **Noogurisa ki?** (what are you selling?).
**Nikinuura** means “it’s tasty”: **ki-** agrees with ekintu-type nouns. For enva (sauce) say **nizinuura**.

culture.title: Milk and eshabwe
body: Ankole is cattle country, famous for its long-horned **Ankole cows**. Milk (**amate**) is drunk fresh or soured, and **eshabwe**, a sauce of whipped ghee and salt, is served with matooke at special meals.
